Basics

Equally likely outcomes

P(A)=∣A∣∣Ω∣P(A) = \frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}P(A)=∣Ω∣∣A∣​

Favourable outcomes over all outcomes.

Symbols: Ω\OmegaΩ: the sample space (all outcomes), AAA: the event, ∣ ∣\lvert\ \rvert∣ ∣: number of outcomes.

The idea

When every outcome has the same chance (a fair die, a well-shuffled deck), the probability of an event is just counting: favourable outcomes divided by all possible outcomes. The hard part is listing Ω\OmegaΩ correctly — with two dice there are 36 ordered outcomes, not 11 sums.

Worked example

One card from a 52-card deck: P(♡)=1352=14P(\heartsuit) = \tfrac{13}{52} = \tfrac14P(♡)=5213​=41​; P(king)=452=113P(\text{king}) = \tfrac{4}{52} = \tfrac1{13}P(king)=524​=131​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Complement

P(Aˉ)=1−P(A)P(\bar A) = 1 - P(A)P(Aˉ)=1−P(A)

Symbols: Aˉ\bar AAˉ: “not AAA”, the event that AAA does not happen.

The idea

“Not AAA” happens exactly when AAA does not, and together they fill Ω\OmegaΩ, so their probabilities add up to 1. When “not AAA” is simpler to count, compute it and subtract from 1.

Worked example

Three coins: “not all tails” is the complement of TTT, so P=1−18=78P = 1 - \tfrac18 = \tfrac78P=1−81​=87​ — much quicker than counting the seven other outcomes.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

At least one

P(X≥1)=1−P(X=0)P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0)P(X≥1)=1−P(X=0)

Symbols: XXX: how many times the event happens.

The idea

“At least one” has many cases (exactly 1, exactly 2, …) but its complement has only one: “none at all”. With independent trials, “none” is a product of probabilities.

Worked example

Four rolls of a die, at least one six: 1−(56)4=1−6251296≈0.5181 - \left(\tfrac56\right)^4 = 1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} \approx 0.5181−(65​)4=1−1296625​≈0.518 — slightly better than even.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Union

P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)

The idea

Adding P(A)P(A)P(A) and P(B)P(B)P(B) counts the overlap twice — subtract it once. In the Venn diagram, the middle lens belongs to both circles.

Worked example

P(A)=0.5P(A) = 0.5P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4P(B) = 0.4P(B)=0.4, P(A∩B)=0.2P(A \cap B) = 0.2P(A∩B)=0.2: P(A∪B)=0.5+0.4−0.2=0.7P(A \cup B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7P(A∪B)=0.5+0.4−0.2=0.7.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Incompatible events

A∩B=∅ ⇒ P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)A \cap B = \varnothing \ \Rightarrow\ P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)A∩B=∅ ⇒ P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)

The idea

If AAA and BBB cannot happen together, there is no overlap to subtract, and the probabilities simply add. Typical case: different values of the same roll.

Worked example

One die, “1 or 6”: the two cannot happen at once, so P=16+16=13P = \tfrac16 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac13P=61​+61​=31​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Geometric probability

P=ℓ(A)ℓ(Ω)P = \frac{\ell(A)}{\ell(\Omega)}P=ℓ(Ω)ℓ(A)​P=S(A)S(Ω)P = \frac{S(A)}{S(\Omega)}P=S(Ω)S(A)​

Use lengths or areas instead of counts.

Symbols: ℓ\ellℓ: a length, SSS: an area.

The idea

When the outcome is a random point (on a segment, in a region), “counting” becomes measuring: the probability is the favourable length or area divided by the total length or area.

Worked example

A point is chosen at random in [0,10][0, 10][0,10]. The chance that it lands in [2,5][2, 5][2,5] is 310\tfrac{3}{10}103​: the length of the target over the length of the whole segment.

Conditional probability

Definition

P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B)P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(A∩B)​

Symbols: P(A∣B)P(A \mid B)P(A∣B): the probability of AAA given that BBB has happened.

The idea

“Given BBB” means we already know BBB happened: BBB becomes the new universe. Inside it, the part where AAA also happens is A∩BA \cap BA∩B, so P(A∣B)P(A \mid B)P(A∣B) is the share of BBB taken by A∩BA \cap BA∩B.

Worked example

P(A∩B)=0.12P(A \cap B) = 0.12P(A∩B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.3P(B) = 0.3P(B)=0.3: P(A∣B)=0.120.3=0.4P(A \mid B) = \tfrac{0.12}{0.3} = 0.4P(A∣B)=0.30.12​=0.4. Knowing BBB raised or lowered the chance of AAA compared to P(A)P(A)P(A).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Multiplication rule

P(A∩B)=P(B) P(A∣B)P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A∣B)

The idea

To get both BBB and AAA: first BBB must happen, then AAA given BBB. Multiply. This is how you handle draws without replacement: each new draw is conditioned on what is already gone.

Worked example

Two cards without replacement, both aces: 452⋅351=1221\tfrac{4}{52}\cdot\tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{221}524​⋅513​=2211​. The second fraction is 351\tfrac{3}{51}513​ because one ace and one card are gone.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Independence

P(A∩B)=P(A) P(B)  ⟺  P(A∣B)=P(A)P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B) \iff P(A \mid B) = P(A)P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)⟺P(A∣B)=P(A)

The idea

AAA and BBB are independent when knowing one does not change the chance of the other: P(A∣B)=P(A)P(A \mid B) = P(A)P(A∣B)=P(A). Equivalently, the probability of both is the product. Do not confuse with incompatible: incompatible events are very dependent.

Worked example

P(A)=0.5P(A) = 0.5P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4P(B) = 0.4P(B)=0.4, P(A∩B)=0.2P(A \cap B) = 0.2P(A∩B)=0.2: since 0.5⋅0.4=0.20.5\cdot 0.4 = 0.20.5⋅0.4=0.2, they are independent. With P(A∩B)=0.3P(A \cap B) = 0.3P(A∩B)=0.3 they would not be.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Total probability

P(A)=∑iP(A∣Bi) P(Bi)P(A) = \sum_i P(A \mid B_i)\,P(B_i)P(A)=i∑​P(A∣Bi​)P(Bi​)

Symbols: B1,B2,…B_1, B_2, \dotsB1​,B2​,…: cases that do not overlap and cover everything.

The idea

Split the world into cases B1,B2,…B_1, B_2, \dotsB1​,B2​,… that cover everything and do not overlap. The chance of AAA is the sum over the cases: probability of the case times probability of AAA in that case — the branches of a tree.

Worked example

Machine M1M_1M1​ makes 60% of the parts with 2% defective; M2M_2M2​ makes 40% with 5% defective. P(D)=0.6⋅0.02+0.4⋅0.05=0.012+0.02=0.032P(D) = 0.6\cdot 0.02 + 0.4\cdot 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.02 = 0.032P(D)=0.6⋅0.02+0.4⋅0.05=0.012+0.02=0.032.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Bayes’ theorem

P(B∣A)=P(A∣B) P(B)P(A)P(B \mid A) = \frac{P(A \mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}P(B∣A)=P(A)P(A∣B)P(B)​

The idea

Bayes turns the question around: from “chance of the effect given the cause” to “chance of the cause given the effect”. The numerator is one path of the tree; the denominator is all paths leading to the observed effect (total probability).

Worked example

Same factory: a part is defective. Which machine made it? P(M2∣D)=0.4⋅0.050.032=0.020.032=0.625P(M_2 \mid D) = \tfrac{0.4\cdot 0.05}{0.032} = \tfrac{0.02}{0.032} = 0.625P(M2​∣D)=0.0320.4⋅0.05​=0.0320.02​=0.625 — the worse machine is more likely, although it makes fewer parts.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Random variables

Expectation

E[X]=∑xi piE[X] = \sum x_i\,p_iE[X]=∑xi​pi​

Symbols: xix_ixi​: the values of XXX, pip_ipi​: their probabilities; E[X]E[X]E[X]: the mean.

The idea

The expectation is the long-run average: each value weighted by its probability. On the bar chart it is the balance point. In games, E>0E > 0E>0 means you win on average.

Worked example

A game: win 10 with probability 0.2, lose 2 otherwise. E=10⋅0.2+(−2)⋅0.8=2−1.6=0.4E = 10\cdot 0.2 + (-2)\cdot 0.8 = 2 - 1.6 = 0.4E=10⋅0.2+(−2)⋅0.8=2−1.6=0.4: on average you gain 0.4 per game.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Variance

Var⁡X=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−E[X]2\operatorname{Var}X = E\left[(X - \mu)^2\right] = E[X^2] - E[X]^2VarX=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−E[X]2σ=Var⁡X\sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}X}σ=VarX​

Symbols: μ=E[X]\mu = E[X]μ=E[X]: the mean; σ\sigmaσ: the standard deviation.

The idea

The variance measures spread: the average squared distance from the mean. The shortcut “mean of the squares minus square of the mean” is usually faster. The standard deviation σ\sigmaσ is its square root, back in the units of XXX.

Worked example

For XXX = 0, 1, 2 with ppp = 0.2, 0.5, 0.3: E[X]=1.1E[X] = 1.1E[X]=1.1, E[X2]=0+0.5+1.2=1.7E[X^2] = 0 + 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7E[X2]=0+0.5+1.2=1.7, so Var⁡X=1.7−1.21=0.49\operatorname{Var}X = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49VarX=1.7−1.21=0.49 and σ=0.7\sigma = 0.7σ=0.7.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Linear change

E[aX+b]=aE[X]+bE[aX + b] = aE[X] + bE[aX+b]=aE[X]+bVar⁡(aX+b)=a2Var⁡X\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}XVar(aX+b)=a2VarX

Symbols: aaa, bbb: constants.

The idea

Shifting by bbb moves the mean but not the spread; scaling by aaa multiplies the mean by aaa and the variance by a2a^2a2 (the standard deviation by ∣a∣\lvert a\rvert∣a∣). A sign change does not reduce the spread.

Worked example

E[X]=3E[X] = 3E[X]=3, Var⁡X=4\operatorname{Var}X = 4VarX=4, Y=2X+1Y = 2X + 1Y=2X+1: E[Y]=7E[Y] = 7E[Y]=7 and Var⁡Y=4⋅4=16\operatorname{Var}Y = 4\cdot 4 = 16VarY=4⋅4=16 — the +1+1+1 does not matter for the variance.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Sums

E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]

Always. For independent variables also Var⁡(X+Y)=Var⁡X+Var⁡Y\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}X + \operatorname{Var}YVar(X+Y)=VarX+VarY.

The idea

Expectations always add, even for dependent variables. Variances add only for independent variables. That is why the mean of many dice grows like nnn while their spread grows only like n\sqrt nn​.

Worked example

Sum of two dice: E=3.5+3.5=7E = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7E=3.5+3.5=7, and since they are independent Var⁡=3512+3512=356\operatorname{Var} = \tfrac{35}{12} + \tfrac{35}{12} = \tfrac{35}{6}Var=1235​+1235​=635​. The bar chart peaks at 7.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

One fair die

E=3.5E = 3.5E=3.5Var⁡=3512\operatorname{Var} = \frac{35}{12}Var=1235​

The idea

Each face has probability 16\tfrac1661​. The mean is the middle of 1 and 6, 3.53.53.5 (never an actual roll!). E[X2]=1+4+9+16+25+366=916E[X^2] = \tfrac{1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36}{6} = \tfrac{91}{6}E[X2]=61+4+9+16+25+36​=691​, so Var⁡=916−3.52=3512\operatorname{Var} = \tfrac{91}{6} - 3.5^2 = \tfrac{35}{12}Var=691​−3.52=1235​.

Worked example

Win as many euros as the die shows, paying 4 to play: the gain is X−4X - 4X−4, so E=3.5−4=−0.5E = 3.5 - 4 = -0.5E=3.5−4=−0.5 — on average you lose 50 cents a game.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Distributions

Binomial B(n, p)

P(X=k)=(nk)pk(1−p)n−kP(X = k) = \binom nk p^k(1 - p)^{n-k}P(X=k)=(kn​)pk(1−p)n−kE=np,Var⁡=np(1−p)E = np, \quad \operatorname{Var} = np(1 - p)E=np,Var=np(1−p)

Symbols: nnn: number of trials, ppp: probability of success in each, kkk: number of successes.

The idea

nnn independent trials, each a success with probability ppp. Exactly kkk successes: choose which kkk trials succeed ((nk)\binom nk(kn​) ways), times pkp^kpk for them and (1−p)n−k(1 - p)^{n-k}(1−p)n−k for the others. On average npnpnp successes.

Worked example

A die rolled 4 times, exactly two sixes: (42)(16)2(56)2=6⋅251296≈0.116\binom42\left(\tfrac16\right)^2\left(\tfrac56\right)^2 = 6\cdot\tfrac{25}{1296} \approx 0.116(24​)(61​)2(65​)2=6⋅129625​≈0.116.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Geometric

P(X=k)=(1−p)k−1pP(X = k) = (1 - p)^{k-1}pP(X=k)=(1−p)k−1pE=1pE = \frac1pE=p1​

Number of trials until the first success: on average 6 rolls to get a six.

Symbols: ppp: probability of success in each trial, kkk: the trial on which the first success comes.

The idea

Repeat a trial until the first success: k−1k - 1k−1 failures, then a success. The probabilities shrink by the factor 1−p1 - p1−p each time. The mean waiting time is 1p\tfrac1pp1​: 6 rolls on average to see a six.

Worked example

First six on the 3rd roll: two failures then a success, (56)2⋅16=25216≈0.116\left(\tfrac56\right)^2\cdot\tfrac16 = \tfrac{25}{216} \approx 0.116(65​)2⋅61​=21625​≈0.116.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Uniform on {1, …, n}

P(X=k)=1nP(X = k) = \frac1nP(X=k)=n1​E=n+12E = \frac{n + 1}{2}E=2n+1​

The idea

Every value 1,…,n1, \dots, n1,…,n is equally likely, like a fair die with nnn faces. The mean is the middle, n+12\tfrac{n + 1}{2}2n+1​. Probabilities of events are counts divided by nnn.

Worked example

A random integer from 1 to 10: E=5.5E = 5.5E=5.5; P(prime)=410P(\text{prime}) = \tfrac{4}{10}P(prime)=104​ (2, 3, 5, 7).

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Normal N(μ, σ²)

Z=X−μσ∼N(0,1)Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0, 1)Z=σX−μ​∼N(0,1)

About 68%68\%68%, 95%95\%95%, 99.7%99.7\%99.7% within 1σ1\sigma1σ, 2σ2\sigma2σ, 3σ3\sigma3σ.

Symbols: μ\muμ: the mean, σ\sigmaσ: the standard deviation; ZZZ: the standard normal variable.

The idea

The bell curve, centred at μ\muμ, with width σ\sigmaσ. Every normal becomes the standard one by measuring “how many σ\sigmaσ away from μ\muμ”: Z=X−μσZ = \tfrac{X - \mu}\sigmaZ=σX−μ​. Rough rule: 68% within one σ\sigmaσ, 95% within two, 99.7% within three.

Worked example

Heights N(170,102)N(170, 10^2)N(170,102): 180 cm is z=1z = 1z=1, so P(X<180)=Φ(1)≈0.841P(X < 180) = \Phi(1) \approx 0.841P(X<180)=Φ(1)≈0.841: about 84% are shorter.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Poisson

P(X=k)=e−λλkk!P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}P(X=k)=e−λk!λk​E=Var⁡=λE = \operatorname{Var} = \lambdaE=Var=λ

Symbols: λ\lambdaλ (lambda): the average number of events in the interval.

The idea

Counts of rare, independent events in a fixed time or space (calls per minute, typos per page), with average λ\lambdaλ. Mean and variance are both λ\lambdaλ. It is the limit of a binomial with large nnn and small ppp, λ=np\lambda = npλ=np.

Worked example

On average 2 calls a minute: the chance of no call in a given minute is e−2≈0.135e^{-2} \approx 0.135e−2≈0.135, and of exactly one call 2e−2≈0.2712e^{-2} \approx 0.2712e−2≈0.271.

Continuous distributions

Density

f(x)≥0f(x) \ge 0f(x)≥0∫−∞∞f(x) dx=1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=1P(a≤X≤b)=∫abf(x) dxP(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dxP(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​f(x)dx

Symbols: fff: the density function; probability is area under it.

The idea

For a continuous variable, single values have probability 0; probabilities are areas under the density curve. So the curve must never go below 0 and the total area must be 1 — that condition usually fixes an unknown constant.

Worked example

f(x)=kxf(x) = kxf(x)=kx on [0,2][0, 2][0,2]: the area is a triangle 12⋅2⋅2k=2k=1\tfrac12\cdot 2\cdot 2k = 2k = 121​⋅2⋅2k=2k=1, so k=12k = \tfrac12k=21​. Then P(0.5≤X≤1.5)=∫0.51.5x2 dx=12P(0.5 \le X \le 1.5) = \int_{0.5}^{1.5}\tfrac x2\,dx = \tfrac12P(0.5≤X≤1.5)=∫0.51.5​2x​dx=21​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Distribution function

F(x)=P(X≤x)=∫−∞xf(t) dtF(x) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dtF(x)=P(X≤x)=∫−∞x​f(t)dtF′=fF' = fF′=f

The idea

F(x)F(x)F(x) is the probability of being at most xxx: the area under the density up to xxx. It climbs from 0 to 1 and never goes down; its slope is the density. The median is where F=12F = \tfrac12F=21​.

Worked example

f(x)=2xf(x) = 2xf(x)=2x on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]: F(x)=x2F(x) = x^2F(x)=x2, so P(X≤0.5)=0.25P(X \le 0.5) = 0.25P(X≤0.5)=0.25 and the median solves x2=12x^2 = \tfrac12x2=21​: x=12≈0.707x = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707x=2​1​≈0.707.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Expectation and variance

E[X]=∫xf(x) dxE[X] = \int x f(x)\,dxE[X]=∫xf(x)dxVar⁡X=∫x2f(x) dx−E[X]2\operatorname{Var}X = \int x^2 f(x)\,dx - E[X]^2VarX=∫x2f(x)dx−E[X]2

The idea

The same formulas as in the discrete case, with sums replaced by integrals: xxx weighted by the density. The mean is the balance point of the area under fff.

Worked example

f(x)=2xf(x) = 2xf(x)=2x on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]: E=∫012x2 dx=23E = \int_0^1 2x^2\,dx = \tfrac23E=∫01​2x2dx=32​, E[X2]=∫012x3 dx=12E[X^2] = \int_0^1 2x^3\,dx = \tfrac12E[X2]=∫01​2x3dx=21​, so Var⁡=12−49=118\operatorname{Var} = \tfrac12 - \tfrac49 = \tfrac1{18}Var=21​−94​=181​.

Uniform on [a, b]

f=1b−af = \frac{1}{b - a}f=b−a1​E=a+b2E = \frac{a + b}{2}E=2a+b​Var⁡=(b−a)212\operatorname{Var} = \frac{(b - a)^2}{12}Var=12(b−a)2​

The idea

Every point of [a,b][a, b][a,b] is equally likely: the density is a flat rectangle of height 1b−a\tfrac{1}{b - a}b−a1​, so probabilities are just lengths over b−ab - ab−a. The mean is the midpoint; the variance is (b−a)212\tfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}12(b−a)2​.

Worked example

Uniform on [2,8][2, 8][2,8]: height 16\tfrac1661​; E=5E = 5E=5; Var⁡=3612=3\operatorname{Var} = \tfrac{36}{12} = 3Var=1236​=3; P(X<4)=26=13P(X < 4) = \tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac13P(X<4)=62​=31​.

Exponential

f(x)=λe−λx (x≥0)f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\ (x \ge 0)f(x)=λe−λx (x≥0)P(X>t)=e−λtP(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}P(X>t)=e−λtE=1λE = \frac1\lambdaE=λ1​

Symbols: λ\lambdaλ: the rate (average number of events per unit of time).

The idea

Waiting times and lifetimes without wear: the density decays like e−λxe^{-\lambda x}e−λx. The chance of surviving past ttt is e−λte^{-\lambda t}e−λt, and the mean lifetime is 1λ\tfrac1\lambdaλ1​. It has no memory: having waited does not shorten the remaining wait.

Worked example

λ=0.5\lambda = 0.5λ=0.5 (mean 2): P(X>2)=e−1≈0.368P(X > 2) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368P(X>2)=e−1≈0.368 — the shaded tail. Even an average lifetime is exceeded only 37% of the time.

Using the normal distribution

Standardising

P(a<X<b)=Φ(b−μσ)−Φ(a−μσ)P(a < X < b) = \Phi\left(\frac{b - \mu}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi\left(\frac{a - \mu}{\sigma}\right)P(a<X<b)=Φ(σb−μ​)−Φ(σa−μ​)

Φ\PhiΦ is the table of N(0,1)N(0, 1)N(0,1): Φ(z)=P(Z≤z)\Phi(z) = P(Z \le z)Φ(z)=P(Z≤z).

The idea

To use the Φ\PhiΦ table, turn each bound into a zzz-score (subtract μ\muμ, divide by σ\sigmaσ). A probability between two bounds is the difference of the two table values.

Worked example

X∼N(50,52)X \sim N(50, 5^2)X∼N(50,52): P(45<X<60)=Φ(2)−Φ(−1)=0.9772−0.1587=0.8186P(45 < X < 60) = \Phi(2) - \Phi(-1) = 0.9772 - 0.1587 = 0.8186P(45<X<60)=Φ(2)−Φ(−1)=0.9772−0.1587=0.8186.

Symmetry

Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z)\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z)P(∣Z∣≤z)=2Φ(z)−1P(|Z| \le z) = 2\Phi(z) - 1P(∣Z∣≤z)=2Φ(z)−1

The idea

Tables only give Φ\PhiΦ for positive zzz. The bell is symmetric, so the left tail at −z-z−z equals the right tail at zzz: Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z)\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z). For a central interval, remove both tails: 2Φ(z)−12\Phi(z) - 12Φ(z)−1.

Worked example

Φ(−1.2)=1−Φ(1.2)=1−0.8849=0.1151\Phi(-1.2) = 1 - \Phi(1.2) = 1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151Φ(−1.2)=1−Φ(1.2)=1−0.8849=0.1151: the small left tail in the picture.

Key values

Φ(1.645)≈0.95\Phi(1.645) \approx 0.95Φ(1.645)≈0.95Φ(1.96)≈0.975\Phi(1.96) \approx 0.975Φ(1.96)≈0.975Φ(2.576)≈0.995\Phi(2.576) \approx 0.995Φ(2.576)≈0.995

The idea

Three numbers worth memorising: 1.6451.6451.645 leaves 5% in one tail, 1.961.961.96 leaves 2.5% in each tail (95% in the middle), 2.5762.5762.576 leaves 0.5% in each tail (99% in the middle). They appear in every confidence interval and test.

Worked example

95% of a normal population lies within μ±1.96σ\mu \pm 1.96\sigmaμ±1.96σ. With μ=100\mu = 100μ=100, σ=15\sigma = 15σ=15: from 70.670.670.6 to 129.4129.4129.4.

Normal approximation to the binomial

B(n,p)≈N(np, np(1−p))B(n, p) \approx N\big(np,\ np(1 - p)\big)B(n,p)≈N(np, np(1−p))

When np≥5np \ge 5np≥5 and n(1−p)≥5n(1 - p) \ge 5n(1−p)≥5. Continuity correction: P(X≤k)≈Φ(k+0.5−npnp(1−p))P(X \le k) \approx \Phi\left(\frac{k + 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{np(1 - p)}}\right)P(X≤k)≈Φ(np(1−p)​k+0.5−np​).

The idea

For large nnn the binomial bars look like a bell with the same mean npnpnp and variance np(1−p)np(1 - p)np(1−p). Each bar covers an interval of width 1, so add 0.50.50.5 to the bound (continuity correction) before standardising.

Worked example

n=100n = 100n=100 coins: μ=50\mu = 50μ=50, σ=5\sigma = 5σ=5. P(X≤55)≈Φ(55.5−505)=Φ(1.1)≈0.864P(X \le 55) \approx \Phi\left(\tfrac{55.5 - 50}{5}\right) = \Phi(1.1) \approx 0.864P(X≤55)≈Φ(555.5−50​)=Φ(1.1)≈0.864.

Mean of a sample

Xˉ∼N(μ, σ2n)\bar X \sim N\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)Xˉ∼N(μ, nσ2​)xˉ±zα/2σn\bar x \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}xˉ±zα/2​n​σ​

The second formula is the confidence interval for μ (z = 1.96 for 95 %).

Symbols: nnn: the sample size, Xˉ\bar XXˉ: the sample mean, zα/2z_{\alpha/2}zα/2​: the critical value for confidence 1−α1 - \alpha1−α.

The idea

Averaging nnn observations keeps the mean μ\muμ but shrinks the spread by n\sqrt nn​: σ/n\sigma/\sqrt nσ/n​, the standard error. That is why a 95% confidence interval for μ\muμ is xˉ±1.96σn\bar x \pm 1.96\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}xˉ±1.96n​σ​ — four times the sample size halves its width.

Worked example

σ=12\sigma = 12σ=12, n=36n = 36n=36: the standard error is 222, so a 95% interval is xˉ±1.96⋅2=xˉ±3.92\bar x \pm 1.96\cdot 2 = \bar x \pm 3.92xˉ±1.96⋅2=xˉ±3.92.

Reading conditional probabilities

P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B)P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(A∩B)​

Inside cell divided by the total of its column (or row, for the other condition).

The idea

“Given BBB” restricts you to the BBB column: divide the cell by the column total. “Given AAA” restricts you to the AAA row: divide by the row total. The most common mistake is dividing by the wrong total.

Worked example

P(A∣B)=0.30.45=23P(A \mid B) = \tfrac{0.3}{0.45} = \tfrac23P(A∣B)=0.450.3​=32​: two thirds of the BBB column is in row AAA.

Tree diagrams

P(A∩B)=P(A) P(B∣A)P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B∣A)P(B)=P(A)P(B∣A)+P(Aˉ)P(B∣Aˉ)P(B) = P(A)P(B \mid A) + P(\bar A)P(B \mid \bar A)P(B)=P(A)P(B∣A)+P(Aˉ)P(B∣Aˉ)

Multiply along a path, add the paths that end in the same event.

The idea

Each branch carries a probability; the branches leaving a node add up to 1. Multiply along a path to get the probability of that whole path; add the paths that end in the same event (total probability).

Worked example

Rain with probability 0.3; late with 0.4 if it rains, 0.1 if not. P(late)=0.3⋅0.4+0.7⋅0.1=0.12+0.07=0.19P(\text{late}) = 0.3\cdot 0.4 + 0.7\cdot 0.1 = 0.12 + 0.07 = 0.19P(late)=0.3⋅0.4+0.7⋅0.1=0.12+0.07=0.19.

Classic facts

Two dice

P(Σ=7)=636=16P(\Sigma = 7) = \frac{6}{36} = \frac16P(Σ=7)=366​=61​

Sum sss (2≤s≤122 \le s \le 122≤s≤12) happens in 6−∣s−7∣6 - \lvert s - 7\rvert6−∣s−7∣ ways.

Symbols: Σ\SigmaΣ: the sum of the two dice.

The idea

Of the 36 equally likely pairs, the sum 7 appears 6 times — along a diagonal of the grid — more than any other sum. The number of ways falls by one for each step away from 7.

Worked example

Sum 9: 6−∣9−7∣=46 - \lvert 9 - 7\rvert = 46−∣9−7∣=4 ways — (3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)(3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3)(3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3) — so P=436=19P = \tfrac{4}{36} = \tfrac19P=364​=91​.

Birthday problem

1−365⋅364⋯(365−n+1)365n1 - \frac{365\cdot364\cdots(365 - n + 1)}{365^n}1−365n365⋅364⋯(365−n+1)​

Probability that two of n people share a birthday: over 50% from n = 23.

The idea

Count the complement: everyone has a different birthday. The first person can have any day, the second must avoid one day, the third two days… With 23 people the chance of a shared birthday already passes 50% — because there are 253 pairs.

Worked example

With n=23n = 23n=23: 1−365⋅364⋯34336523≈0.5071 - \tfrac{365\cdot 364\cdots 343}{365^{23}} \approx 0.5071−36523365⋅364⋯343​≈0.507. With 50 people it is already about 97%.

Drawing without replacement

P=(Kk)(N−Kn−k)(Nn)P = \frac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N - K}{n - k}}{\binom Nn}P=(nN​)(kK​)(n−kN−K​)​

kkk special items among nnn drawn from NNN, of which KKK are special (hypergeometric).

The idea

Draw nnn items at once from NNN, of which KKK are special. Count the favourable hands: choose kkk of the special ones and n−kn - kn−k of the others, then divide by all possible hands (Nn)\binom Nn(nN​) (the hypergeometric law).

Worked example

5 cards, exactly 2 aces: (42)(483)(525)=6⋅172962598960≈0.040\tfrac{\binom42\binom{48}{3}}{\binom{52}{5}} = \tfrac{6\cdot 17296}{2598960} \approx 0.040(552​)(24​)(348​)​=25989606⋅17296​≈0.040.
